products.title: UnReflectAnything
products.subtitle: RGB-only highlight removal by rendering synthetic specular supervision
products.description: RGB-only highlight removal by rendering synthetic specular supervision.

blocks.text: Specular highlights distort appearance, obscure texture, and hinder geometric reasoning in both natural and surgical imagery. We present UnReflectAnything, an RGB-only framework that removes highlights from a single image by predicting a highlight map together with a reflection-free diffuse reconstruction. The model uses a frozen vision transformer encoder to extract multi-scale features, a lightweight head to localize specular regions, and a token-level inpainting module that restores corrupted feature patches before producing the final diffuse image. To overcome the lack of paired supervision, we introduce a Virtual Highlight Synthesis pipeline that renders physically plausible specularities using monocular geometry, Fresnel-aware shading, and randomized lighting, enabling training on arbitrary RGB images with correct geometric structure. UnReflectAnything generalizes across natural and surgical domains and achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks.

Specular highlights arise from mirror-like reflections on non-Lambertian surfaces, producing saturated, view-dependent artifacts that obscure scene content and corrupt downstream perception tasks such as segmentation, correspondence, and photometric inference. In natural images, these highlights distort color fidelity and degrade restoration or relighting pipelines. In endoscopic scenes, bodily fluids, moist tissue, and strong non-uniform lighting introduce intense specularities that occlude anatomy, bias texture cues, and hinder navigation and decision-making. Such artifacts critically impair depth estimation, optical flow, and stereo reconstruction in surgical robotics, where accurate scene understanding is essential and visual ambiguity can carry clinical impact.

blocks.caption: Fig. 1. UnReflectAnything removes specular highlights from a single RGB image with no paired supervision: a Virtual Highlight Synthesis pipeline renders physically plausible highlights onto arbitrary images to create the training pairs.

blocks.text: We integrate physically grounded virtual highlight synthesis with token-space inpainting to recover reflection-free images from a single RGB view. Given an input image, monocular geometry is estimated to obtain metric depth, surface normals, and intrinsics; a point light is sampled in camera space and a Blinn–Phong lobe with Fresnel modulation renders synthetic specularities on top of the real image, producing paired supervision without multi-view capture or polarization. A frozen ViT encoder extracts multi-scale features; a DPT-based highlight head localizes specular regions, corrupted tokens are inpainted, and a diffuse decoder reconstructs the reflection-free output. The full pipeline is trained end-to-end on synthetically highlighted images and transfers to unseen real domains at inference.

blocks.caption: Fig. 2. Synthetic highlight generation. Per-pixel depth and surface normals are estimated from a single RGB image, a point light is sampled in camera space, and a Blinn-Phong/Fresnel term renders the highlight layer.
Fig. 3. Model architecture: a frozen DINOv3 encoder E, a highlight-localization head H, token-space inpainting over the masked features, and a DPT decoder D reconstructing the diffuse image.

blocks.text: UnReflectAnything is evaluated on datasets with paired diffuse-only ground truth (PSD, SHIQ, SSHR) and on surgical endoscopy, where it consistently suppresses and attenuates specular highlights while preserving structure. Across natural-scene benchmarks it matches or exceeds state-of-the-art diffusion and physics-based baselines on MSE, PSNR, and SSIM, and in challenging endoscopic scenes it avoids the over-dimming and residual highlights common to diffusion methods. Ablations confirm the contribution of virtual highlight synthesis, token inpainting, and the Fresnel-aware rendering model. The feedforward architecture runs in real time on a single consumer GPU, making deployment more plausible than iterative diffusion alternatives.

blocks.caption: Fig. 6. Qualitative results: raw input (left) against the UnReflectAnything reconstruction (right), across natural scenes and surgical endoscopy.

blocks.text: UnReflectAnything demonstrates that RGB-only highlight removal is feasible when training is driven by physically plausible synthetic supervision rather than paired real captures. The framework generalizes from natural images to surgical endoscopy, where conservative reconstruction over hallucination is clinically desirable. Remaining limitations include reduced reliability on transparent or refractive objects, where diffuse and specular components are difficult to separate; future work may extend the synthesis model to handle such materials.

products.title: SCALE-EM
products.subtitle: Self-supervised embeddings for endoscopic matching
products.description: Self-Supervised Contrastive Embedding Adaptation for Endoscopic Image Matching.

blocks.text: Accurate spatial understanding is essential for image-guided surgery, augmented reality integration, and context awareness. In minimally invasive procedures, establishing precise pixel-level correspondences between endoscopic frames is critical for 3D reconstruction, camera tracking, and scene interpretation. However, weak perspective cues, non-Lambertian tissue reflections, and deformable anatomy degrade conventional computer vision techniques. This work presents a deep learning pipeline for endoscopic feature matching alongside a self-supervised optimization framework: a novel-view synthesis pipeline generates ground-truth inlier correspondences used to mine triplets within a contrastive learning paradigm, augmenting a frozen DINOv2 backbone with an additional Transformer layer optimized for cosine-similarity matching.

Minimally invasive surgery has revolutionized modern practice by reducing patient trauma and recovery times, but restricted vision and limited tactile feedback increase technical complexity. Real-time computer vision on the endoscopic feed can provide AR overlays, tool tracking, and 3D reconstruction, all of which depend on robust feature matching between frames. The surgical environment poses unique challenges: non-rigid tissue deformation, dynamic lighting, specular reflections, smoke, and blood make general-purpose descriptors insufficient. This investigation adapts pretrained vision transformer representations to produce matchable patch embeddings for endoscopic imagery without manual annotation.

The pipeline augments a frozen DINOv2 backbone Φ with a trainable adaptation layer Ψ. Pseudo-ground-truth correspondences are generated via novel-view synthesis: a source frame is back-projected into 3D using a monocular depth estimate, transformed with a randomly sampled rigid motion, and re-projected to synthesize a warped target view; pixel mappings between source and warped views provide geometrically consistent supervision. Triplets (anchor, positive, negative) are mined in embedding space and optimized with contrastive (triplet) loss so matching points lie close while non-matches are pushed apart. At inference, correspondences are extracted via cosine similarity with mutual nearest-neighbor matching and refined to sub-pixel precision with Fourier phase correlation.

blocks.caption: Fig. 1. Architecture: a frozen DINOv2 backbone Φ maps both frames into a semantic feature space; the trainable adapter Ψ projects them into a matching space where correspondences are recovered by cosine similarity and argmax.

Fig. 2. Pseudo-ground-truth generation. A source frame is back-projected with a monocular depth estimate, moved by a random rigid transform and re-projected, yielding dense correspondences with no manual labels.

blocks.text: On the SCARED stereo endoscopy test split, SCALE-EM achieves the lowest mean epipolar error among all tested methods (8.63 px, ~17% better than the next-best classical descriptor) and the fewest spurious matches under a cross-sequence robustness test (160 inliers on non-corresponding images vs. thousands for LoFTR and SIFT variants). Ablation studies confirm gains from the adaptation layer Ψ and sub-pixel refinement. The method remains competitive in runtime with other learning-based matchers while prioritizing precision over match density through a conservative scoring mechanism.

blocks.caption: Fig. 4. Pixel correspondences on the SCARED test split: four representative pairs drawn from the two held-out sequences.

blocks.text: SCALE-EM shows that self-supervised contrastive adaptation of foundation-model features can yield precise endoscopic correspondences without manual labels. The approach is most suitable for applications requiring high-precision sparse matching; conservative rejection of ambiguous matches limits density compared to some baselines. Performance depends on the quality of depth maps used for novel-view synthesis, suggesting future work on more robust geometric priors for surgical scenes.

products.title: MESA
products.subtitle: Adnexal Mass Segmentation in US images
products.description: Adapting Foundation Models for Annotation-Efficient Adnexal Mass Segmentation in Cine Images

blocks.text: Adnexal mass evaluation via ultrasound is hindered by subjective interpretation and inter-observer variability. While automated segmentation supports quantitative risk assessment, fully supervised convolutional architectures require large pixel-level annotation budgets and struggle under domain shift. We propose a label-efficient framework leveraging a pretrained DINOv3 foundation backbone integrated with a Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT)-style decoder that hierarchically reassembles multi-scale features. Evaluated on 7,777 annotated frames from 112 patients, the method achieves a Dice score of 0.945 and reduces the 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance by 11.4% relative to the strongest convolutional baseline, while retaining strong performance when trained on only 25% of the data.

Adnexal masses are common in gynecological practice, where the central objective is to distinguish benign from malignant lesions. Diagnostic performance depends on acquisition quality and operator expertise, leading to substantial variability. Ultrasound images are further challenged by speckle noise, acoustic shadowing, and low contrast. Accurate segmentation is a prerequisite for quantitative assessment pipelines including the IOTA ADNEX model and O-RADS risk stratification. Foundation models pretrained on large-scale natural-image corpora offer semantic priors that may transfer to medical ultrasound with minimal task-specific pretraining.

blocks.caption: Fig. 1. (a) Predicted masks against ground truth on adnexal ultrasound cine frames; (b, c) metric comparison across architectures and behaviour as the annotation budget shrinks.

blocks.text: Grayscale cine frames are mapped to pseudo-RGB via channel replication and passed through a frozen DINOv3 encoder; a DPT-style decoder hierarchically reassembles features from layers {F₃, F₆, F₉, F₁₂} into a binary segmentation mask. Only the decoder is trained under a combined BCE and Dice objective (λ_BCE = 0.3, λ_Dice = 0.7) with AdamW, cosine learning-rate schedule, and 224×224 inputs. Baselines include U-Net, U-Net++, DeepLabV3, and MAnet trained under identical protocols. Data-starvation experiments train on 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of the labeled set to assess annotation efficiency.

blocks.caption: Fig. 2. Architecture: a frozen DINOv3 encoder extracts hierarchical features that a DPT-style decoder resamples and reassembles into the binary segmentation mask.

blocks.text: MESA reaches Dice 0.945 and the best boundary-sensitive metrics across resolutions 224×224 and 512×512, outperforming all convolutional baselines on IoU, sensitivity, and Hausdorff distance. Under data starvation, CNN architectures degrade sharply at 25% of labels while the DINOv3-based model retains substantially higher Dice and lower HD95. Ablations across DINOv3 scales (Small, Base, Large, Giant) reveal early performance saturation and overfitting at extreme scales, with moderately sized backbones offering the best accuracy–efficiency trade-off for boundary-sensitive ovarian ultrasound segmentation.

blocks.caption: Fig. 4. Efficiency analysis: segmentation quality against model capacity (a), and against the fraction of labels withheld (b).

blocks.text: Integrating a self-supervised DINOv3 backbone with a DPT decoder delivers state-of-the-art adnexal mass segmentation with markedly improved contour fidelity and resilience to limited annotations. The findings support foundation-model priors as a practical path toward annotation-efficient deployment in clinical ultrasound workflows, where expert labels are costly and inter-operator variability is high.

products.title: Spectra-BREAST
products.subtitle: 3D Hyperspectral Mapping of Lumpectomy Specimens
products.description: A Lightweight Fiducial-Based Pipeline for 3D Hyperspectral Mapping of ex-vivo Lumpectomy Specimens

blocks.text: Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) is promising for intraoperative assessment of resection margins in breast-conserving surgery, but clinical translation requires aligning 2D spectral information onto the 3D shape of excised tissue so suspicious regions can be precisely localized. We present a fully automated, calibration-free pipeline that produces a 3D hyperspectral point cloud of an ex-vivo lumpectomy specimen from consumer-camera RGB images and a single top-down HSI acquisition. Evaluated on two specimens, the pipeline achieves median 3D registration error below 1 mm and 2D reprojection error below 0.02 mm, with per-specimen processing under 4 minutes.

Breast-conserving surgery is standard for early-stage breast cancer, but positive margins occur in 10–70% of cases and drive reoperation in ~20% of patients. Margin assessment currently relies on postoperative histopathology, while intraoperative alternatives are slower or less accurate for whole-specimen evaluation. HSI has shown high classification accuracy on breast tissue, yet existing approaches produce only 2D spectral maps, neglecting 3D geometry that clinicians use when deciding which regions require targeted follow-up.

The pipeline inputs N RGB images and one top-down HSI cube acquired with four planar ArUco markers around the specimen. 3D geometry is recovered with a deep-learning Structure-from-Motion backbone (MASt3R-SfM) and stabilized in a metric frame via custom bundle adjustment enforcing consistency on 16 ArUco corners. HSI registration avoids recovering the HSI camera pose: shared markers define corner correspondences that drive a planar homography, and 3D coordinates are recovered by lookup on an orthographically rendered depth map. The output is a spectral point cloud C ∈ ℝ^(S×(B+3)) with metric coordinates and full spectral signatures per surface point.

blocks.caption: Fig. 1. The registration pipeline: N RGB images and one HSI cube, four planar ArUco markers, MASt3R-SfM geometry, ray-casting onto the mesh, and a 2D-2D registration with depth lookup.

blocks.text: On specimens SB019 and SB020, 2D reprojection error stays below 0.02 mm (mean ± std: 0.017 ± 0.009 and 0.013 ± 0.003 mm over 16 corners). Median 3D registration error is 0.945 mm [IQR 0.731–1.378] for SB019 and 0.974 mm [IQR 0.753–1.088] for SB020. End-to-end processing completes in under 4 minutes per specimen (3D reconstruction ~3 min; 2D–3D registration ~24 s on an NVIDIA A100), supporting intraoperative timing constraints.

blocks.caption: Fig. 2. Left: 3D registration median error and total compute time. Right: 2D median reprojection error, both as a function of the fraction of RGB images used.

blocks.text: This is, to our knowledge, the first HSI–3D fusion for lumpectomy specimens achieved without dedicated geometric hardware or cross-modal pose estimation. Sub-millimeter registration and sub-4-minute runtime support feasibility for HSI-guided spatial localization in margin assessment. Limitations include evaluation on only two specimens and ground truth derived from the same photogrammetric reconstruction; independent 3D landmark validation remains future work.

products.title: muVES
products.subtitle: 3D analysis of microvasculature on-chip
products.description: A three-dimensional method for morphological analysis and flow velocity estimation in microvasculature on-a-chip.

institutions.name: Fondazione IRCCS Istituto Nazionale dei Tumori

blocks.text: Three-dimensional imaging (e.g., confocal microscopy) is commonly used to visualize microvasculature-on-a-chip models, yet 3D analysis is not standard for extracting quantitative metrics. We developed μVES to compute morphological parameters (radius, length, tortuosity, eccentricity) and intravascular flow velocity from segmented 3D volumes. Applied to fibrin-gel microvascular networks, the tool reproduces literature-consistent capillary morphology and, combined with bead-tracking velocimetry, estimates flow velocities and wall shear stresses that agree with experiments under imposed pressure gradients.

Microfluidic microvasculature-on-a-chip models study angiogenesis, tumor extravasation, immune recruitment, and drug delivery with increased physiological relevance from human-derived cells and 3D architecture. Perfusion under controlled pressure enables functional readouts, but most morphological analyses still rely on 2D projections of confocal stacks, discarding information along the vessel axis and mis-estimating radius and surface-to-volume ratios when cross-sections are non-circular.

μVES comprises eight steps: acquisition, preprocessing (cubic voxel interpolation, optional downsampling), segmentation (active contours or a deep-learning alternative), network alignment, skeletonization, branch splitting, per-branch morphometry, and Poiseuille-based flow solving over the vascular graph under an assumed pressure drop. Wall shear stress is derived from velocity and local radius. A 2D projection mode (μVES2D) enables validation against REAVER and manual tracing before full 3D analysis.

blocks.caption: Fig. 3. The μVES pipeline, from confocal acquisition to morphometry and flow: preprocessing, segmentation, alignment, skeletonization and branch processing.

blocks.text: Validated against REAVER on 2D projections, μVES matches established length estimates before exploiting the full volume, where mean vessel eccentricity is 0.833 ± 0.125, revealing markedly non-circular cross-sections invisible to 2D analysis (2D mean radius 41.3 μm vs. 3D 28.5 μm on a representative network). Across 30 microvascular networks, mean capillary diameter is 31.4 ± 16.2 μm and tortuosity 1.18, consistent with in vitro literature. Flow velocities under 100/200/400 Pa pressure gradients agree with bead-tracking measurements; wall shear stress remains lower than in vivo references but approaches physiological values at higher imposed gradients. Deep-learning segmentation cuts computation time substantially with comparable morphological output.

blocks.caption: Fig. 2. Network reconstruction and the radius / length distributions under 2D, downsampled-3D and full-3D analysis: 2D markedly overestimates vessel radius.
Fig. 5. Functional velocity evaluation on a perfused network: flowrate, fluid velocity and wall shear stresses solved over the vascular graph, against experimental measurements.

blocks.text: μVES demonstrates that 3D analysis is essential for accurate microvascular morphometry and functional assessment in vitro. The open-source MATLAB implementation enables reproducible characterization of vasculature-on-a-chip models and highlights where current in vitro networks match or diverge from in vivo microvasculature in morphology and hemodynamics.

products.title: STEVE
products.subtitle: Augmented training curriculum for surgical robotics
products.description: Implementation and assessment of an augmented training curriculum for surgical robotics.

blocks.text: High-level haptic assistance algorithms integrated into surgical robotics training may help aspiring surgeons build a more comprehensive skillset and improve clinical performance. This work presents a haptic-enhanced VR simulator for surgical robotics training with eight physics-based tasks, augmented by force-based guidance that redirects the trainee's hands toward targets or away from obstacles and provides quantitative performance scores. An experimental study shows that augmented assistance improves training performance and promotes skill transfer to unassisted scenarios resembling clinical teleoperation.

The growth of robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery demands trained surgeons capable of teleoperating complex systems safely. Haptic assistance (HA) at the leader manipulator can redirect hand motion through forces and torques, potentially accelerating skill acquisition in virtual training environments where tasks are customizable and performance quantifiable. This work studies HA in the context of a structured curriculum paired with the da Vinci Research Kit, evaluating whether assisted training improves both in-simulation performance and transfer to novel unassisted tasks.

STEVE implements four HA strategies (trajectory guidance, obstacle avoidance, surface guidance, and insertion guidance) as visco-elastic force/torque fields on the master manipulators. Eight Unity tasks span training (Path, Rings, Pillars, Exchange) and evaluation (Liver Resection, Thymectomy, Nephrectomy, Suturing) scenarios targeting wrist articulation, depth perception, hand-eye coordination, and bimanual exchange. Performance P is a task-weighted combination of distance error, angular error, force/torque magnitudes, instrument drops, and repositioning time, normalized to expert execution. Eight novice subjects were randomized to assisted or control groups: four days of thrice-daily assisted or unassisted training, two rest days, then unassisted evaluation on unseen tasks.

blocks.caption: Fig. 1. The four haptic assistance strategies as visco-elastic force/torque fields: (a) trajectory guidance, (b) obstacle avoidance, (c) surface guidance, (d) insertion guidance.
Fig. 2. The eight simulated tasks. Blue headers mark the training tasks; orange marks the realistic evaluation tasks, performed by both groups without assistance.

blocks.text: During training, the assisted group consistently outperformed controls across all four training tasks with improving trends over repetitions. On day-7 evaluation tasks, executed without assistance by both groups, assisted subjects achieved higher median performance on Thymectomy (+13.07%), Liver Resection (+21.54%), and Suturing (+8.44%), with only Nephrectomy showing a slight decrease (−2.71%). The results suggest HA during training improves unassisted performance on novel surgical-like tasks, supporting skill transfer through integrated visuo-haptic feedback during teleoperation.

Haptic-enhanced VR training on a surgical robot simulator improves task performance during assisted practice and may transfer to unassisted clinical-like scenarios. Extensions include adaptive visco-elastic parameters, larger cohorts, and long-term retention studies. STEVE provides an open hardware/software stack for replicating augmented surgical robotics curricula.

products.title: UnderXAI-OVIT
products.subtitle: Decision support in ovarian cancer treatment
products.description: Deep Learning for decision support in ovarian cancer treatment planning.

institutions.name: Università degli Studi Magna Graecia di Catanzaro

blocks.text: Ovarian cancer is the deadliest gynecologic malignancy, with complete resection after primary debulking surgery associated with the most favorable prognosis, yet assessing resectability at diagnosis remains challenging. We propose OVIT, a fully automated decision support system predicting residual tumor after primary debulking from preoperative CT and clinical variables, without manual segmentation or expert radiological scoring. On an independent test cohort of 75 patients from a 465-patient retrospective HGSOC cohort, the best model achieves AUC 0.80 (95% CI: 0.68–0.89) and recall 0.86 (95% CI: 0.71–0.97), correctly identifying 24 of 28 non-resectable cases including 13 of 14 intraoperatively aborted surgeries.

High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma is often diagnosed at advanced FIGO stage III–IV with widespread abdominal dissemination. The choice between primary debulking surgery (PDS) and neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by interval debulking is made in multidisciplinary tumor boards using criteria on anatomical dissemination and surgical feasibility, yet unforeseen unresectability discovered intraoperatively remains a critical failure mode. Automated prediction from routinely available preoperative CT and biomarkers could flag patients unlikely to benefit from PDS before surgery.

blocks.caption: Fig. 1. Segmentation masks for two subjects in each resectability group: pelvic and ovarian lesions in yellow, omental disease in green, across the three anatomical planes.

blocks.text: Preoperative contrast-enhanced CT volumes are automatically segmented into pelvic/ovarian and omental lesion masks by an open-source model, converted to 2D slices, and encoded slice-by-slice with a frozen pretrained Vision Transformer. Per-slice classification tokens are aggregated with an attention module and fused with clinical variables (age, CA125, HE4) through a lightweight MLP classification head; only the fusion and classification layers are trained. Four ViT backbones (DINOv2-small/base, Google-16/32) are compared with and without clinical fusion on a 390/75 train/test split from the European Institute of Oncology cohort.

blocks.caption: Fig. 4. OVIT architecture: CT volumes are cut into 2D slices, a frozen ViT encodes each slice, an attention module pools the slice tokens, and clinical variables are fused before the MLP classifier.

blocks.text: The Google-32 ViT encoder with clinical fusion achieves the best test performance: AUC 0.80, recall 0.86, correctly flagging 86% of non-resectable patients including 93% of surgeries aborted intraoperatively for unforeseen unresectable disease. Ablations show clinical-variable benefit is architecture-dependent: Google-32 gains most from multimodal fusion on recall-oriented metrics. Misclassifications link false negatives to older, lower-biomarker patients and false positives to elevated HE4 and higher surgical complexity scores.

blocks.caption: Fig. 2. Resectability classification against the previously proposed model: confusion counts on the left, AUC / accuracy / precision / recall / F1 on the right.

blocks.text: OVIT demonstrates that frozen ViT encoders with attention pooling and clinical fusion can predict ovarian cancer resectability without manual radiological scoring. High recall on non-resectable cases supports its role as a decision-support tool to identify patients who may not benefit from primary surgery, pending prospective validation and integration into multidisciplinary workflows as part of the Under-XAI project.

products.title: Robotic Colonoscopy
products.subtitle: Patient-specific digital-twin world models
products.description: Coverage-Optimal Robotic Colonoscopy via Patient-Specific Digital-Twin World Models

blocks.text: Post-colonoscopy interval cancers account for 2–8% of colorectal cancers, driven primarily by mucosa that goes unexamined during withdrawal. The Adenoma Detection Rate (ADR) is inversely associated with interval-cancer risk, yet current robotic colonoscopy systems optimize for reaching the caecum rather than maximizing patient-specific mucosal coverage. We propose patient-specific digital-twin world models that segment a CT colonography scan into an individualized colon environment where a navigation agent learns coverage-optimal policies rewarded for novel mucosal coverage weighted by view quality.

Colonoscopy is the reference test for colorectal-cancer screening, yet interval malignancies emerge when lesions present during examination are missed. ADR is the strongest validated quality indicator and is dose-dependently linked to interval-cancer risk. A primary cause of misses is mucosa hidden behind haustral folds or at flexures. Recent autonomous colonoscopy systems advance locomotion and caecal intubation but do not optimize how completely the colonic surface is inspected, leaving completeness operator-dependent and unmeasured.

A patient's CT colonography scan is segmented into a patient-specific digital twin providing full surface geometry so mucosal coverage along any trajectory is exactly measurable. Inside the twin, a world model predicts the next state S(t) = [RGB, T, C%]ₜ (endoluminal view, camera pose, and cumulative coverage) from each candidate action A(t). A navigation policy is trained in a closed loop against reward R(θ) = ΔC% · q(d, α), crediting novel coverage gain ΔC% weighted by view quality q that penalizes large viewing distance d and oblique incidence angle α. The trained policy transfers to robotic shared-autonomy deployment on the live endoscopic feed with the clinician in the loop.

blocks.caption: Fig. 1. The pipeline: a CT colonography scan becomes a patient-specific digital twin; inside it a world model predicts the next endoluminal view, pose and cumulative coverage, and the policy is rewarded for novel coverage weighted by view quality.

blocks.text: The framework is evaluated by mucosal coverage percentage, ADR, and number of missed lesions, metrics aligned with the clinical failure mode of inadequate inspection. Beyond aggregate scores, the digital twin yields per-patient blind-spot maps localizing hard-to-visualize regions and coverage-optimal inspection plans tailored to each colon's anatomy, standardizing inspection quality and reducing operator dependence.

By reframing autonomous colonoscopy around mucosal coverage rather than caecal reach, patient-specific digital-twin world models directly target a root cause of interval cancers. The approach received the Best Poster Award at the Hamlyn Symposium workshop on Physics- and AI-Driven Digital Twins for Patient-Specific Robotic Diagnosis, Interventions and Therapies (sponsored by NVIDIA).

products.title: Surgical AR Review
products.subtitle: Recent advancements in AR for robotic surgery
products.description: Recent advancements in augmented reality for robotic applications: a survey.

blocks.text: Robots are expanding from industrial applications to daily life, and augmented reality (AR) has been integrated into many robotic applications across medical and industrial domains. This survey reviews AR for medical robots in preoperative and surgical task planning, image-guided robotic surgery, surgical training and simulation, and telesurgery; and for industrial robots in human–robot interaction and collaboration, path planning and task allocation, training and simulation, and teleoperation control/assistance. Limitations, challenges, and future perspectives are discussed for researchers working at the intersection of AR and robotics.

Robotic systems have become prevalent in medical and industrial applications, offering high positioning accuracy, improved dexterity, and reduced trauma in surgery, and productivity and consistency in manufacturing. AR can transcend physical interaction limits by integrating holographic information onto real scenarios, improving situational awareness before and during task execution. This review synthesizes how AR has been applied to medical and industrial robotic systems, organizing the literature by application theme and identifying cross-cutting challenges.

blocks.caption: Fig. 1. AR in medical and industrial robotic applications: visualization and guidance for robot-assisted surgery (left), and for industrial manipulation tasks (right).

blocks.text: The survey follows a structured literature review across two domains. Medical robotics is organized into four themes: (1) preoperative and surgical task planning with CT/MRI registration and port placement optimization; (2) image-guided robotic surgery with rigid and deformable registration on da Vinci and custom platforms; (3) surgical training and simulation including AR-guided curricula and haptic augmentation; and (4) telesurgery covering remote visualization, teleoperation, and latency mitigation via predictive displays and digital twins. Industrial robotics is reviewed across human–robot collaboration, path planning, training/simulation, and teleoperation, spanning HMD, projector-, and tablet-based AR on platforms from HoloLens to KUKA and Universal Robots.

Across medical AR robotics, preoperative planning applications improve target localization and robot configuration; image-guided surgery overlays span rigid orthopedics to deformable abdominal procedures; training systems demonstrate skill acquisition benefits with AR feedback; and telesurgery work addresses latency through predictive displays. In industrial settings, AR assists gesture-, gaze-, and BCI-driven collaboration, intuitive path planning and programming, mixed-reality training, and teleoperation with virtual fixtures. Common findings include trade-offs between registration accuracy, field of view, hardware ergonomics, and cognitive load across both domains.

AR holds promise for improving operator awareness in robotic applications, but immersion, hardware comfort, registration accuracy, safety, communication latency, and simulation-to-real transfer remain open challenges. Future directions include more ergonomic displays, multimodal interaction (haptic, audio, gaze), reduced hardware cost as consumer AR matures, and tighter integration of digital twins for predictive assistance in both surgical and industrial teleoperation.

products.title: GroundControl
products.subtitle: Monitor your hardware from your terminal, all of it at the same time.
products.description: Rich visualization and monitoring of system metrics in the terminal.

details.body:
Ground Control is a Textual TUI that turns any terminal into a live cockpit for the machine you are on: per-core CPU, RAM and swap, temperatures, per-mount disk I/O, network throughput and NVIDIA GPU telemetry, all redrawn together on one screen. It needs no display server and no browser, so a headless workstation or an HPC login node is watched over SSH exactly the way a laptop is.

It is not only a TUI. The same collectors back `gc --once`, which takes a single sample and exits as text, as JSON, or as a Nagios-style exit code, so cron, CI and monitoring agents can read the same numbers the dashboard draws.
highlights: Runs over SSH: no display server, no browser, no agent to install
CPU, memory, temperature, per-mount disk I/O, network and NVIDIA GPU on one synchronized screen
Slurm-aware: focus a job and every panel reports from inside its allocation, tail its output, cancel it
Grid, horizontal and vertical layouts, one keystroke apart and sized for a tmux split
Twenty built-in themes plus a colour picker that previews on live data
Threshold alerts marked ▲ / ■, so they survive a monochrome terminal
`gc --once --json` and `--check` for cron, CI and Nagios-style monitoring

blocks.text: Every panel the machine has to offer is on screen at once in the grid layout. `h` and `v` re-flow the same widgets into a single row or a single column, which is what a horizontal or vertical tmux split actually wants. The switch is instant and the history in each plot is preserved.

blocks.alt: Ground Control switching between grid and horizontal layouts
blocks.caption: Grid → horizontal → grid with `g` and `h`, on live data.

items: CPU: per-core load as horizontal bars, with frequency and colour-coded intensity
Memory: RAM on the positive axis, swap on the negative, with a used/free centre bar
Temperature: up to four sensors over time, with warning bands at 60 °C and 80 °C
Disk: read/write throughput and used/free space, one widget per mounted partition
Network: upload and download rates plus cumulative transfer
GPU: utilization and memory for NVIDIA cards, with power draw, clocks and throttle reasons
Slurm: your running and pending jobs, shown wherever `squeue` is on PATH

blocks.caption: The GPU widget: utilization against memory, with a telemetry line for power, clocks and throttling.

blocks.text: Any panel that crosses a threshold paints its border and prefixes its title with a marker: ▲ for a warning, ■ for critical. The marker matters as much as the colour: it survives a monochrome terminal. Thresholds are written as plain numbers, because direction is a property of the metric, and a breach stays visible for a few seconds after recovery so a spike is not missed while you are on another tab.

blocks.caption: A breach marks the panel and holds the marker briefly after recovery.

blocks.text: `gc --once` takes one sample, prints it and exits: no alternate screen, no event loop. `--json` makes it machine-readable with a `schema_version`, and `--check` returns the Nagios convention (0 ok, 1 warn, 2 crit, 3 collector failed) so it drops into an existing monitoring setup unchanged. `gc --stream` emits one compact JSON object per line for continuous collection.

blocks.caption: `gc --once`: the same collectors, without the dashboard.

products.title: sekrt
products.subtitle: Your secrets: synced, retrievable and safely stored. Plus a painless way to keep .env files out of your repos.
products.description: An AES-256 secret manager with a Textual TUI, first-class .env and SSH-key workflows, and sync through any private git remote.

details.body:
sekrt is a secret manager for developers and DevOps engineers: `pass`, but with a modern Textual interface, first-class support for API keys, SSH keypairs and `.env` files, and sync through any private git remote you already have. Every entry is an independent file encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key derived from your passphrase with scrypt.

Three dependencies, no daemon, no sudo and no GPG keyring to set up. The vault is a plain git repository, so `sekrt sync` is a pull and a push, and a second machine gets everything by cloning it.
highlights: Passwords and API keys in folders, generated on demand, copied to a clipboard that clears after 45 s
`.env` files encrypted per repository, and restored into any fresh clone with one command
`sekrt run` hands a command its secrets in that process's environment only, for as long as it runs
SSH keypairs imported, generated (ed25519) and restored with the right permissions
Git sync: every change is a commit, and the remote only ever sees ciphertext
TUI and CLI, with inline pickers and forms when you leave an argument out
Three dependencies, no daemon, no sudo, no GPG setup

blocks.text: `sekrt init` creates a vault at `~/.local/share/sekrt` and asks for the passphrase that will encrypt it. Commands that touch a secret ask for that passphrase; `ls`, `find`, `rm` and `status` never do, because they decrypt nothing. `sekrt unlock` caches the derived key (never the passphrase) in a RAM-backed, user-private location with a TTL: gpg-agent, without the agent.

blocks.caption: Init, add, get: a working vault in four commands.

blocks.text: `sekrt env push` encrypts the `.env` of the repository you are standing in and files it under that repo; `sekrt env pull` restores it in any fresh clone, on any machine. Monorepos with one env file per service are handled, and an edited local file is never overwritten without `--force`.

blocks.caption: A repo's .env, encrypted into the vault and restored in a fresh clone.

sections.title: Running a command with your secrets

blocks.text: `sekrt expose` cannot work, because a child process cannot set variables in the shell that started it. So sekrt wraps the command instead, and the values live in *its* environment for exactly as long as it runs. Never written to disk, never left in your shell, and never placed in a command line, because `ps` is world-readable. `sekrt shell` opens a subshell that tags its own prompt, so a shell holding secrets never looks like an ordinary one.

blocks.caption: `sekrt run` and `sekrt shell`: secrets scoped to one process.

blocks.text: `sekrt` with no arguments opens the interface: a folder tree of the vault, fuzzy filtering, a masked detail view, add and edit forms with a built-in generator, and one-key sync. Eleven colour presets, one per hue, editable live with `t`.

blocks.caption: Browsing, filtering, revealing and syncing, without leaving the keyboard.

items: AES-256-GCM per entry; key derived with scrypt (N=2¹⁵, r=8, p=1) and a random per-vault salt
The entry's logical name is the GCM associated data, so a renamed or moved ciphertext fails to decrypt
The remote sees names, folder structure and timestamps; contents are always ciphertext
`unlock` caches the derived key in tmpfs (0600, wiped on logout), never the passphrase
Clipboard clears after 45 s, and only if it still holds the copied value
$SEKRT_PASSPHRASE is stripped from wrapped children, so they cannot decrypt anything they were not handed

products.title: dasshboard-tui
products.subtitle: Moving between SSH hosts just got a whole lot easier.
products.description: A home screen for your terminal: every host in your SSH config becomes a tile you can open with one key.

details.body:
dasshboard is a home screen for your terminal. Every host in `~/.ssh/config`, plus anything you add yourself, including plain local commands, becomes a tile. Pick one and it connects, in this terminal, a new tab or a new window.

Everything is editable from inside the TUI; there is no `$EDITOR` handoff. `~/.ssh/config` is never written to: editing one of its hosts writes an override block into dasshboard's own `config.toml` that merges on top of it.
highlights: Reads `~/.ssh/config` and turns every host into a tile: nothing to declare twice
`1`–`9` opens a numbered tile; `⏎` opens the selected one
Add, edit, duplicate, hide, recolour and reorder tiles without leaving the TUI
`/` finds a host by name, target or jump host
Jump hosts, per-tile working directory and per-tile command (`tmux attach`, a login shell, anything)
Groups and section headings, drawn in the order you set
Written in Rust with ratatui; runs on macOS, Linux, BSD and Windows Terminal

blocks.text: Arrows or `hjkl` move, `g` and `G` jump to the first and last tile, `⏎` opens. `t`, `w` and `c` override where a session lands (a new tab, a new window, or this terminal) for one launch, without changing the default.

blocks.caption: Moving between tiles, then opening one in this terminal.

blocks.text: `/` filters by name, target or jump host. `a`, `e` and `d` add, edit and duplicate a tile; `D` deletes one after asking; `x` hides it and `X` brings every hidden tile back. Edits rewrite whole blocks as text, so the comments and formatting in your config survive, and a TOML error is reported in the status line rather than taking the board down.

blocks.caption: `/` matches against name, target and jump host.
Adding a host from inside the TUI: `~/.ssh/config` is never written to.

blocks.text: `S` manages groups: a section heading with an ordered list of tiles under it. `s` opens settings: whether to include `~/.ssh/config`, whether hidden tiles show at startup, where sessions open, and the two theme colours. Every host gets a colour, auto-assigned unless you pick one.

blocks.caption: Sections group the board and are drawn in the order you set.
Primary and accent colours, applied live.

blocks.text: The TUI runs anywhere, and opening a session in the current terminal works everywhere. Opening a new tab or window needs a terminal with an automation interface, which today means Ghostty ≥ 1.2 on macOS, where the new surface also picks up the host's colour as a tint. Everywhere else `tab` and `window` resolve to `current`, so a shared config still parses and still works.

products.title: dotfiles
products.subtitle: This is what you install if you want your terminal to look like mine.
products.description: One line to set up a new machine: tmux, oh-my-posh, Claude Code, Neovim and a pile of portable shell additions.

details.body:
tmux, Claude Code, oh-my-posh, herdr and a pile of portable shell additions, kept in step across a laptop, a workstation and a couple of HPC login nodes. On a machine with nothing on it, one line is the whole thing. The script clones the repo, hands over to the copy inside it, and falls back to a release tarball where git is not installed yet.

Sudo is detected, not assumed. The installer works out whether you are root, have passwordless sudo, are a sudoer who has to type a password, or have no sudo at all, and picks its install routes accordingly: system package manager where there is privilege, rustup, `uv tool install`, release tarballs or conda-forge where there is not.
highlights: `curl -fsSL albertorota.dev/setmeup.sh | bash` on a machine with nothing on it
A setup UI whose preview panes are the real thing: the actual prompt, status bar and install plan, not a drawing
Colour and machine name land in templates, rendered into `.generated/` and symlinked, so tracked files stay machine-agnostic
Every path it touches is recorded in a manifest, and any file already there is moved aside to `.bak`
`reset.sh` reads the manifest back and undoes exactly what was done
No-sudo machines get the full catalogue through userland routes
bash and zsh from one file, on both Linux and macOS, down to bash 3.2

blocks.text: `install.sh` installs uv first, because the setup UI is itself a uv script, then opens it: two accent colours, the machine name, which pills belong in the status bars, and which tools to put on the machine. The panes on the right are real: the prompt is `oh-my-posh print` on a rendered copy of the actual template, the status bar is the string the installer assembles with its `#(...)` segments really executed, and the install plan is the same route resolution the run performs. A machine without uv, or without the network to fetch it, falls back to a plain text wizard.

blocks.caption: The setup UI: colours, machine name, status-bar pills and the tool catalogue.

sections.title: What it does to the machine

blocks.text: Anything carrying a colour or the machine name is a `*.in` template with `@PRIMARY@`-style placeholders, because tmux.conf, JSON and TOML cannot indirect through a variable. Each one is rendered into `.generated/` and the real config path is pointed at the rendered copy, so `~` still shows what is managed and re-running the installer updates live config. A real file already sitting at a path is moved to `<file>.bak`, once, and a backup is never written over.

blocks.alt: install.sh rendering templates and linking them
blocks.caption: Templates rendered into `.generated/`, then symlinked into place.

blocks.text: Installing puts a `dotfiles` CLI on PATH, so none of this needs the checkout to be your working directory again. It is a wrapper rather than a second implementation: every subcommand runs `install.sh`, `reset.sh` or `lib/tools.sh` out of the checkout, and options pass straight through.

blocks.caption: `dotfiles` wraps the scripts in the checkout; it does not reimplement them.

blocks.text: `reset.sh` reads the manifest back, removes everything on it, restores each path's `.bak` and strips the block it added to `~/.bashrc` and `~/.zshrc`. Numbered backups it reports and leaves alone, since choosing between several saved files is a human's job. It undoes config, not software: the tools stay installed.

blocks.caption: Uninstall walks the manifest backwards and puts the `.bak` files back.

items: shell: tmux, oh-my-posh, jq, zoxide, eza, fzf, fd, bat, delta, glow, dua-cli
network: Tailscale (installed, not connected: `tailscale up` is left to you)
gpu: nvitop
editor: Neovim with LazyVim, Claude Code
python: gdown, ground-control-tui
herdr: herdr, herdr-statusline, herdr-file-viewer
toolchains: git, Rust, a C toolchain, Homebrew, conda-forge, each only if something needs it

products.title: DaSSHboard
products.subtitle: A stylish SSH dashboard for VS Code
products.description: One-click access to your SSH hosts, WSL distros and running Docker containers, from a customizable VS Code panel.

details.body:
DaSSHboard turns the cluttered remote menu in VS Code into a visual launcher. It reads `~/.ssh/config` for your SSH hosts, detects WSL distros, and parses `docker ps` for running containers, then puts every one of them a single click away, along with each of the folders you actually work in on them.

Works in VS Code, Cursor and Windsurf, and is published on both the VS Marketplace and Open VSX.
highlights: SSH hosts, WSL distros and Docker containers in one panel
Several entrypoint folders per host, each one click from either window
Grid or list layout, toggled from the panel, the context menu or settings
A colour and a Lucide icon per host, and a colour per section
Right-click anything (path, host card, section, background) for a menu that fits it
Labels for long paths, with the full path one hover away
Discovery is resilient: a slow DNS lookup or an unresponsive `wsl.exe` times out instead of blocking

blocks.text: Hit the DaSSHboard button in the status bar, use the Remote menu, or run "Show DaSSHboard" from the Command Palette. Each host card lists the entrypoint paths on that host, with buttons to open one in the current window or a new one. Opened from inside a remote session, it also offers a Close connection button, coloured for the kind of remote you are in.

blocks.alt: The DaSSHboard panel in VS Code
blocks.caption: Every remote environment, one click away.

blocks.text: Grid or list, switched with the toggle at the bottom of the view, from the right-click menu, or with the `daSSHboard.layout` setting.

blocks.caption: Grid layout.
List layout.

blocks.text: Click the icon on a host card to give it its own colour and one of the Lucide icons, so a host is recognizable before you read its name. Sections get a colour of their own from the square next to the title, or from `settings.json`. Not happy with a look? Reset icon & color puts it back to the theme default.

blocks.alt: Choosing a host icon in DaSSHboard
blocks.caption: A colour and an icon per host.

blocks.alt: Choosing a section colour in DaSSHboard
blocks.caption: A colour per section: SSH, WSL and Docker.

WSL distro: the default user's home directory of that installation
Docker container: the container root, fixed
A host with no usable default shows an Add entrypoint row rather than a phantom path

products.title: MedView
products.subtitle: NIfTI / DICOM viewer for VS Code
products.description: A NIfTI and DICOM viewer that runs inside VS Code, with multi-planar reconstruction and segmentation overlays.

details.body:
MedView lets clinicians and engineers inspect NIfTI (`.nii`, `.nii.gz`) and DICOM (`.dcm`) volumes inside VS Code: no separate viewer, no context switch out of the pipeline you are debugging. It registers as the default editor for those extensions, so opening the file is all it takes.

Volumes are streamed to the viewer as binary and decoded in a background worker using native gzip, so a 330 MB compressed CT (a 760 MB volume) opens in seconds and the interface stays responsive.
highlights: Axial, sagittal and coronal views of the same volume
Segmentation overlays, discovered automatically next to the image and in its subfolders
Per-label colours with voxel counts; click a label to hide or show it
Fill or outline rendering with an opacity slider, and a refusal to overlay a mismatched grid
Brightness and contrast, rotation and flips, all applied live
Native resolution with no interpolation, and physical aspect ratio from the voxel spacing
Arrow keys, Page Up/Down, Home/End and the mouse wheel to move through slices

blocks.text: The same volume in all three anatomical planes, with global intensity normalization so brightness is consistent across slices and voxel spacing respected so proportions are anatomically right.

blocks.caption: Axial.
Sagittal.
Coronal.

blocks.text: MedView looks for label volumes next to the image and in its subfolders, so a layout like `case/CT.nii.gz` plus `case/ovseg_predictions/CT.nii.gz` is picked up with no configuration; Browse… covers anything it misses. Labels are listed with their voxel counts and their own colours, rendered filled or as outlines, and a label volume whose grid does not match the image is refused rather than silently misaligned.
